sentences.text: Camposaurus was a small, meat-eating theropod dinosaur.
Scientists estimate this animal grew to be about 3 meters long.
Like its relatives, it possessed fused ankle bones known as tibio-tarsals and fibulo-tarsals.
However, unlike other members of its group, a specific ridge ran along the rear of the tibia to connect with the fibula.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as UCMP 34498, was found in 1934 at the Placerias quarry within the Bluewater Creek Formation in Arizona.
Although discovered decades earlier, the species Camposaurus arizonensis was not formally named until 1998 by Adrian Hunt and colleagues.
The genus name translates to "Camp's lizard" in honor of Charles Lewis Camp.
Many paleontologists initially rejected the name as a nomen dubium due to a lack of fossil material.
In 2000, Downs examined the remains and concluded it was a junior synonym of Coelophysis.
A 2007 review by Nesbitt et al. noted that the ventral astragalar margin was straight and indistinguishable from that of Coelophysis bauri.
Later, a reassessment by Ezcurra and Brusatte revealed two autapomorphies in the holotype, firmly establishing it as a valid genus and species.
Analysis confirmed that Camposaurus is definitely a neotheropod.
It belongs to the parent group Coelophysinae and is classified in the family Coelophysidae.
A 2011 phylogenetic analysis found Camposaurus to be a close relative of Megapnosaurus rhodesiensis.
A 2017 phylogenetic analysis found the synonymy with Coelophysis unsupported, placing Camposaurus in a clade with Megapnosaurus, Segisaurus, and Lucianovenator.
Camposaurus lived during the early to middle Norian stage of the Late Triassic period.
This corresponds to a time between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
